Nor should it be understood that this world was created by any intelligent being;
for if there were a creator of this universe, he would have to be either eternal or non-eternal.

In that regard, an eternal creator is not tenable, because if an eternal and capable creator existed, it would follow that creation, maintenance, and dissolution would necessarily occur simultaneously.

If it is argued that since the very nature by which he is the agent of maintenance and dissolution is present even at the time of creation, he would therefore effect maintenance and dissolution at that very time,

and that he does not do so only because of the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), that is incorrect; for he is never deprived of a permanent auxiliary cause, since such a cause is always present.

Nor is it devoid of impermanent auxiliary causes, because even those impermanent auxiliaries have their production dependent upon that [permanent cause]; consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of all effects being produced at once.
[Objection: But this fault does not apply, since God possesses intelligence (*buddhimattva*).
For one devoid of intelligence would produce an effect arising from its own mere existence simultaneously;

but as for the intelligent one, although capable of acting, he does not act because he lacks the desire to do so—what blame can there be for him? It is replied: even those desires are dependent upon his own mere existence; "why does he produce them?"—this indeed is the blame directed at him.

If it is argued that even though its capacity exists by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), this is simply its inherent character (*svabhāva*)—namely, that it does not act without an adventitious power (*āgantuka-śakti*) characterized as a "cooperative cause" (*sahakārin*)—then you would also have to say of a barren woman that she is barren by her very nature even while being a mother; thus, this argument is trivial. Now, if you say: "This is indeed the nature of the effect (*kārya-svabhāva*): it does not arise from the capable [cause] alone, but occurs only subsequently in dependence upon a cooperative cause; therefore, there is no reproach against it"—that is not tenable. For a capable [cause], disregarding the need for a cooperative cause, ought to produce the effect by its own force alone.
Otherwise, it would follow that this [cause] lacks causal capacity;

nor is it logical that a permanent entity produces effects sequentially, because it is independent [of other conditions]. As Dharmakīrti, whose fame is renowned throughout the quarters of the world, has said: "Because a permanent entity is independent, sequential production is not tenable."

By the statement, "In both action and non-action, the self remains identical in nature throughout the two times," the successive production of effects by non-momentary entities such as the self and others, as well as by momentary entities such as pots and the like, has been refuted.
Nor is there a contradiction with perception here, because it is impossible for perception to apprehend the non-momentary;
for momentary perception is not capable of perceiving what is non-momentary,
since the non-momentary necessarily involves an operation across multiple moments.
How can that [object] be apprehended by a perception occurring at a single moment?
For its prior and subsequent existence is not manifested now; otherwise, it would follow that even those [prior and subsequent states) would possess the nature of being present.

Because it would entail the appearance [of the object] persisting until its birth and destruction, this [cognition] is not perception; it is incapable of grasping any object that pervades prior and subsequent times.
By this, the non-perceptual nature of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is explained, for perception is a cognition that is direct (*sākṣātkārin*).
Nor is the previous state to be directly perceived now; rather, it is to be remembered.
Furthermore, the nature of memory is not perception.

Now, if it is argued that this would be memory if it did not directly perceive the present state, then how can that which is inclined toward direct perception be called "memory"? As Bhaṭṭa said: "Memory arises as 'it' with respect to that which was previously cognized."
But this recognition, namely "this is that very same thing," is something additional;
therefore,

Because recollection is impossible when there is direct apprehension, and direct apprehension is impossible when there is recollection;
furthermore, recollection and direct apprehension cannot both belong to a single [cognition] because they are mutually contradictory.
For it is impossible for one who is not insane to claim that the very form by which there is recollection is the same form by which there is direct apprehension.
Furthermore, if a single entity were both remembered and perceived through different forms,
then even while it exists, there would be both perception and non-perception;
however, in the case of what is being remembered, there can be no perception at all, because perception is impossible [with respect to a remembered object].
Therefore, the cognition of recognition is indeed erroneous because it lacks a real object;

and the formal argument is as follows: whatever is a cognition of recognition does not, in reality, have a single object, just like the cognition of recognition regarding grass that has been cut down and grown again;
and this cognition "this very same blue thing" is likewise a cognition of recognition—this is the perception of a pervader of the contradictory.

Because unity and multiplicity are mutually contradictory, there is also a contradiction between the cognitions that have them as their objects; therefore, by the logic previously stated, the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is pervaded by having multiple objects—a state which is incompatible with having a single object. Thus, recognition does not subvert the inference of momentariness.
Furthermore, even in the case of [the illusion of] hair and the like, there is no state of having a single object, since it has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object.
Since it is precisely the manifestation of the hair and so forth that is being recognized,
if it were the universal (*sāmānya*) that is being recognized, the cognition would have to be "this is that very hair-ness," and not "this is that very hair.

Therefore, since there is a contradiction in the production of the recognition-cognition— whether sequentially or otherwise— if it were based on a single object, one should not suspect the fallacies of contradiction (*viruddha*) or inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).

Now, if this manifesting entity is indeed cognition alone, then from where does the existence of an external object follow? The establishment of an external object must occur through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*); for blue and other forms do not manifest everywhere and at all times, and this would not be possible if they were produced solely by the power of their own material cause (*svopādāna*).

Since activity toward a restricted object would otherwise be impossible, it must be concluded that there exists for these [cognitions] some cause distinct from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), by whose power they arise at certain times and in certain places; and that very thing is the external object. However, this external object is not a "whole" (*avayavin*), nor are those properties such as qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, which are held by others to reside in substances (*dravya*), nor the ninefold substance, nor even atoms.
Among these, it cannot be the qualities and so forth, because they are already negated by the negation of the substance itself.
Furthermore, since inherence cannot exist in the absence of an inherent substance (*samavāyidravya*), that objection is not considered here.
Substance is of nine kinds: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind.

This cognition of "I" is occasional; thus, in terms of its meaning, it is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
This reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because the property of being a cognition is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the subject (*dharmin*), which is the "I"-cognition.
Nor is the qualification "occasional" unestablished, because there is no cognition of "I" at all times.
Nor is it contradictory, because it is observed in similar instances (sapakṣa);

Furthermore, if occasional cognition were to arise from a non-occasional cause, it would follow that it could never fail to arise from its occasional cause.

Furthermore, if there were an indeterminate cause, it would follow that there is no cause at all. Moreover, if [the reason] were inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), then even well-established reasons such as smoke would be inconclusive, since there would be no distinction [between them].

Alternatively, even when it is active, it would result in its having the nature of being inactive, because that is its very essence.

Therefore, even the mind does not exist at all;
what remains are earth and the other elements, and these are held to be twofold, distinguished as composite wholes and atoms.

In this regard, it has been stated that the non-perception of a well-known whole (*avayavin*), such as a jar, which is composed of atoms through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, and which meets the conditions for perceptibility, constitutes a sublation (*bādhaka*).

If it is asked, "If the whole does not exist, how then does it appear as a single entity?"—the answer is: it is merely the parts that appear, arranged in such and such a manner; however, no partless possessor of those parts (*tadvat*) is ever perceived.
Thus it has been said.

Now, what indeed is this so-called "appearance of parts"? If it is simply the appearance of atoms accumulated by occupying various directions and locations, then how can it be said in the *Dharmottara* that "grossness is a property of the appearance"? For there too, this is precisely the meaning.
There is no cognition of an object in its own essential form; for it is said that "the cognition of an object is figurative.
Therefore, the very appearance of blue and so forth which is experienced as pervading various locations is itself the appearance of grossness, and thus there is no fault.

Furthermore, those atoms which are the constituents of that [gross object]—which, in the view of the Vaiśeṣikas, are the direct objects of perception; in the system of the Vaibhāṣikas, are the actual objects of sensory experience; and in the opinion of the Sautrāntikas, are inclined toward imparting their own forms [to consciousness]—these too are not possible in the view of the Yogācāras.

Indeed, a single atom cannot maintain its established status, because for that which resides in the center of atoms situated above, below, and in the four cardinal directions, it necessarily follows that it possesses six parts;
for that very nature of it which is adjacent to the eastern atom cannot logically be the same as that which is adjacent to the western atom.
Because they would have to occupy the same location,
it follows that if that atom situated next to the preceding atom were to approach the subsequent atom, the latter too would have to be in that very place;
even if there were no actual proximity, this same situation would apply even in the case of mere facing toward one another.
Consequently, it follows that the aggregate is merely of the size of an atom; for it is only the parts that appear arranged in such and such a manner,
and no further partless whole possessing them is ever perceived.

[This is] neutral, or rather, this is the investigation: that which appears here as such cannot reasonably be one, because of the investigation just mentioned.
Nor is it manifold, because an atom cannot exist as a plurality of atoms;

for instance, if it were composed of parts, how could it be an atom? If, on the other hand, it were partless, then when atoms are joined, they would occupy the same location as one another due to their conjunction in their entirety, and thus every aggregate would be no more than a single atom—meaning even a mountain or the entire earth would be so.
Therefore, a distinction between these two natures must necessarily be admitted.

Just as it is with these two, so too there is a distinction between the natures of atoms situated in the directions of below, above, south, north, and so on; thus, by the force of logic, it follows that the atom must have six parts.
As it has been said: "Because of simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms], the atom would have six parts;
if the six were in the same location, the entire mass would be no larger than a single atom."
Thus, since the one is not established, neither is the many; therefore, atoms do not exist.

If there is no external object, then what is the object of this appearance? Indeed, this appearance, proceeding from beginningless and pervasive latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), is observed to be entirely without an objective basis (*nirālambana*).

For instance: if an object exists, there must be an objective support (*sālambanatā*), and by that [support] there must be either a composite whole (*avayavin*) or an accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu-pracaya*).
Yet both of these have their forms seized by the grasp of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) just mentioned as refutations; they do not differ from a lotus in the sky.
As it has been said: "There is no such thing as a composite whole, nor do atoms exist;
the appearance is without objective support, resembling an experience in a dream."
Dream-cognition is indeed known to be without an objective basis,
and there is no difference whatsoever between the experiences of dreaming and waking,
since they are seen to possess similarity in every respect.
Furthermore, a consciousness that has not acquired a specific form distinct from being objectless is not capable of experiencing a connection with an object;

for whatever is indistinguishable from the objectless is itself objectless, just as a second cognition [of hair] is objectless because it is indistinguishable from the single perception of hair in the sky.
And since the waking consciousness under dispute is indistinguishable from dream-consciousness, which is objectless, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

If external objects do not exist, what then is ultimately real? Ultimate reality is consciousness alone, free from the manifold elaborations (*niṣprapañca*) and unstained by the blemishes of the grasped and the grasper.
As it has been said: "Consciousness, liberated from the grasped and the grasper, is ultimately real.
Furthermore, it has been stated: "There is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there any other experience of that [intellect] itself."
Due to the absence of the grasped and the grasper, that very [consciousness] shines forth by itself;

and this has been stated by the Blessed One: "For no external object exists in the way it is conceptualized by the foolish; rather, the mind, stirred by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), proceeds appearing as an object."
Thus, regarding this, some say as follows: "All this is indeed consciousness alone, established in the form of all bodies and objects;
and since that is self-cognizing, it is neither the grasped nor the grasper for anyone."
However, through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the state of the grasped and the grasper is established;
therefore, consciousness—which is devoid of that imagined state of grasped and grasper—is true as being endowed with aspects (*sākāra*).
Others, however, maintain that the ultimate consciousness is unstained by the blemish of any aspects whatsoever, resembling a pure crystal.
These forms appear as false, manifested by ignorance;

therefore, that which is called the "object of apprehension" (grāhya) does not exist at all. Since the object of apprehension is absent, the state of being an "apprehender" (grāhaka) belonging to consciousness in relation to it also does not exist.
In the view of the Mādhyamikas, however, even that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), because it cannot withstand analysis.
For in the world, that which is endowed with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is said to be ultimate;
yet, when analyzed, no intrinsic nature—whether one or many—is tenable for this [consciousness], because it cannot withstand the aforementioned analysis.
As it has been said: "Even that consciousness is not accepted by the wise as ultimate,
because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, like a lotus in the sky."
Kīrtipāda also said: "The nature by which entities are defined does not exist in reality,
because neither a single nor a manifold nature is found among them."

Likewise, it has been stated by the author of the Alaṅkāra: "But when neither conceptual construction nor anything else possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge, then, even as everything dissolves, who can be at fault? Even the distinction between the bound and the liberated does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality."

"For those who perceive equality everywhere, indeed no difference appears at all"—this is the formal argument (*prayoga*). Furthermore, it is as follows: whatever does not possess the nature of being both one and many is not ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), just like a sky-lotus; and consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not possess the nature of being both one and many. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
This reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*),

because, just as in the case of an external object, the incompatibility of having a nature that is neither one nor many is perfectly clear in the case of cognition possessing an aspect (*sākāra-jñāna*);
for that which is the basis for the world’s conventional usage of "external object" is precisely what the proponent of the theory of aspects (*sākāravādin*) calls "cognition."
Therefore, whatever constitutes a refutation of its existence as something external is itself a refutation of its existence as something internal;
for it is not accepted that this form—which is both gross and manifold—is of the nature of atoms.

Whether this form, consisting of consciousness, is considered a single gross entity or a manifold one differentiated into atoms, in either case, the defects inherent in the position of an external object cannot be avoided.

For there is no defect based on external existence regarding that cognition, by which there might be a sublation caused by corporeality due to its being such [an external thing]; [the claim] that this does not apply to the incorporeal nature of the self as cognition is also hollow,
because if cognition possesses a form, it too is corporeal.
For this very form, which possesses spatial extension, is what is meant by "materiality" (mūrti),
according to the intermediate [view].
